full_name: Praia D'El Rey Golf & Beach Resort

summary.text: A resort course by the American architect Cabell B. Robinson, opened in 1997, that mixes pine-forest holes with dune and clifftop holes on Portugal's Silver Coast.

setting.text: Mixes holes cut through pine forest with holes among sand dunes and along the coast, with views of the Atlantic and the Berlengas Islands.
Set in two clockwise loops of nine. The round starts in thinned-out forest, glimpses the ocean at the 2nd and 3rd, then heads back away from the water until midway through the back nine.
From the 4th the course turns inland for the rest of the front nine.
Top100golfcourses picks out holes 12 to 15 as the stretch that runs along the coast.
Parts of the ground are pure white sand dunes covered in thick ice plant, and the rest is fragrant pine forest.
Planet Golf notes that houses separate the fairways in many areas and occupy some of the prime golf land.
Golf Monthly's Mike Harris found it far more playable than West Cliffs, with a lower chance of losing a ball, though sprawling bunkers and large greens mean it is no pushover.
The resort sits in the Vale de Janelas (Windows Valley), between the fishing town of Peniche to the south and the Óbidos Lagoon to the north.

history.text: Opened in 1997. The club says it was inaugurated on 14 June 1997.

The resort development was first proposed in the late 1970s. Earlier zoning permission let Robinson route holes along the clifftop, which Planet Golf says would no longer be possible in this part of the world.
Cabell B. Robinson spent 20 years working for Robert Trent Jones in Europe before designing it.

After viewing the site, Robinson reportedly said: 'This is the kind of landscape we architects try to create, but at Praia D'El Rey it's all here, naturally. Now it's my responsibility to protect it.'
Golfshake says the original order of play had the coastal holes on the front nine, but the nines were reversed so the most memorable holes come late in the round.
The resort is named after the Serra d'El-Rei, where Peter I of Portugal had a castle in which he met Dona Inês. Two main streets are named after Pedro and Inês.
Wikipedia says the land was bought in the late 1960s by Dutch investors who formed the Beltico Group, and that building work began in the late 1990s.
The resort manages the neighbouring West Cliffs course, which opened in 2017.

trivia.text: NCG's Top 100 European Golf Resorts list placed the Praia D'El Rey resort 6th (page read in October 2026).
Top100golfcourses quotes Gold World calling it 'A mix of holes – some in the mighty dunes, others among fragrant pines – that are an assault to the senses. Wild and wonderful'.
The 17th is 570 metres from the back tees. The Portuguese Tourist Office text on Portugal Golf Courses called it the second longest par 5 in Portugal and one of the longest in Europe.
Wikipedia gives the course as par 73 and 6,625 metres.
Wikipedia says the resort's Marriott hotel is regularly used by Portugal's national football team, who train on the resort's football pitches.
Wikipedia cites the 2008 World Travel Awards, which named the resort Portugal's Leading Resort.

1.text: A par 4 with a right-to-left dogleg and a choice on the tee of how close to the left side to go. The green's length can mean as much as a three-club difference from front to back.

2.text: A par 5 of 463 metres, with water on the right and bunkers and rough ever present.
The resort calls it a classic risk and reward par 5: cutting the corner over the water leaves a relatively short second to a raised green.
Known for its view towards the Berlengas Islands.

3.text: A par 3 that looks simple but can cause problems. The tee shot can be anything from a wedge to a fairway wood, and the long green has two big rollers.

4.text: Planet Golf calls it a terrific reachable par 4.
The resort describes a natural-looking hole with a raised green and a large waste bunker to the left of it.

5.text: The resort calls it probably the toughest par 4 on the course and says a par here should be gratefully accepted.

6.text: Planet Golf calls the 6th green a wicked plateau.
The resort says it is a par 4 dogleg right from a raised tee, with a ridge through the centre of the green.

8.text: A par 3 that normally plays into the wind, with a lake in front of the green and steep slopes and bunkers behind. The resort calls it a signature short hole.

9.text: A par 4 of 393 metres that Top100golfcourses describes as all uphill, with a narrow fairway and nine bunkers.
The resort says it usually plays into the wind and the green is wide and shallow, so the approach plays longer than it looks.

10.text: A par 5 of 460 metres with a tricky green protected by a deep bunker on the left and an even deeper lake on the right.
Played from an elevated tee with a panoramic view, with out of bounds down the left.

11.text: A par 3 that the resort calls the toughest one-shotter on the course. It plays straight uphill, so it plays longer than its distance, and the only safe miss is short.

12.text: A par 5 that the resort calls a links-style hole dog-legging left, with a bunker guarding the left of the green.
Golfmyhome says it runs beside the Atlantic and starts the main coastal sequence.

13.text: A short par 4 with a big view and a birdie chance, but the prevailing wind off the ocean brings the right-hand fairway bunkers into play.

14.text: A par 3 open to the sea breeze, with a long, narrow green and bunkers either side.
Golfmyhome says it deserves particular attention when the wind changes.

15.text: A par 4 with the beach and out of bounds on the left, and a steep downslope that can add distance to a long tee shot.

17.text: A par 5 of 570 metres, a monstrous uphill hole in Top100golfcourses' words.
The resort says it doglegs left with the prevailing wind behind, and that 'a par here feels like a birdie'.

18.text: A par 4 with a right-to-left dogleg. The green sits in a corner guarded by trees, bunkers on the right and a natural dune on the left.

local.text: Sits close to the medieval town of Óbidos, with its Moorish castle and lagoon, about an hour north-west of Lisbon.
Peniche, a fishing town, lies to the south of the resort and the Óbidos Lagoon to the north.
The resort has a Marriott hotel and its beach is open to the general public.
West Cliffs lies about ten minutes north of the resort and is managed by it.
Royal Óbidos is nine minutes away, according to Premier Golf.
Óbidos is a medieval walled town whose walls are almost intact, and tradition says King Dinis gave it to Queen Isabel, which is why it is known as the Town of Queens.
